title: Section 12.1: Three-Dimensional Coordinate Systems
learningObjectives: Identify coordinate planes and the first octant
Plot points in space using ordered triples
Compute distance between points in R^3

sections.title: Overview & Motivation
sections.content: Three-dimensional coordinates extend the familiar plane by adding a third dimension. This section introduces the spatial language you need for vectors, surfaces, and multivariable calculus.

sections.title: The 3D coordinate system
sections.content:
Definition: A point in space is represented by an ordered triple ((x,y,z)) that gives its position along three perpendicular axes.

Explanation: The x-axis measures left-right position, the y-axis measures forward-back position, and the z-axis measures up-down position. Each coordinate is independent.

examples.title: Class example — Plotting a point
examples.prompt: Plot the point in space and describe its movement from the origin.

interactive.prompt: Describe how to move from the origin to the point.

examples.instructorSolution: Start at the origin. Move 2 units in the positive x direction, then 1 unit in the negative y direction, then 3 units upward in the z direction. The point is (2,-1,3).

examples.title: Student practice — Plot this point
examples.prompt: Use an ordered triple to locate the point in space.
examples.instructorSolution: Move 1 unit in the negative x direction, 4 units in the positive y direction, and 0 units in z. The point lies on the xy-plane in the second quadrant direction.

sections.title: Coordinate planes
sections.content:
Definition: The coordinate planes are the three planes formed by pairing two axes and setting the third coordinate to zero.

Explanation: The xy-plane is defined by z=0, the xz-plane by y=0, and the yz-plane by x=0. Points on a plane have no movement in the excluded direction.

examples.title: Class example — Identify the plane
examples.prompt: Which coordinate plane contains the point (3,-2,0)?

interactive.prompt: Look at the coordinates and find the zero coordinate.

examples.instructorSolution: The point has z=0, so it lies in the xy-plane. The x and y coordinates are free, while z stays fixed at zero.

examples.title: Student practice — Identify the plane

interactive.prompt: Find the coordinate that equals zero.

examples.instructorSolution: The x-coordinate is zero, so the point lies in the yz-plane. The point is on the plane where x=0 and can still move in y and z.

sections.title: Distance in space
sections.content:
Definition: The distance between two points in space is the length of the straight line segment connecting them.

Explanation: Use the distance formula in three dimensions: (d=sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2}).

examples.title: Class example — Distance formula
examples.prompt: Compute the distance between P=(1,2,3) and Q=(4,-1,5).

interactive.prompt: Substitute each coordinate difference into the formula.

examples.instructorSolution: Compute differences: Δx=3, Δy=-3, Δz=2. Then d=sqrt{3^2+(-3)^2+2^2}=sqrt{9+9+4}=sqrt{22}.

examples.title: Student practice — Distance formula
examples.prompt: Find the distance between A=(2,0,1) and B=(2,3,5).

interactive.prompt: Check which coordinates change and compute the distance.

examples.instructorSolution: Only y and z change: Δx=0, Δy=3, Δz=4. Distance is sqrt{0^2+3^2+4^2}=5.
